rubric.why: Recognises that the species’ population has declined or is threatened.
rubric.description: States that the species has declining numbers or is threatened.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying decline or threat to the species.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining risk of disappearance.
rubric.description: States that the species is at risk of extinction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the species may become extinct.

modelAnswer: An endangered species is a species whose population has declined so much that it is at risk of extinction.

items.followUp: Give one difference between a primary and a secondary cell wall.

rubric.why: Shows when the primary wall forms or describes its properties.
rubric.description: States that the primary cell wall forms first, while the cell is growing, and is thin and flexible.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct feature of the primary wall.

rubric.why: Shows when the secondary wall forms or describes its properties.
rubric.description: States that the secondary cell wall forms after growth and is thicker and more rigid, often containing lignin.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct feature of the secondary wall.

modelAnswer: The primary cell wall forms first, while the cell is growing; it is thin and flexible.
The secondary cell wall forms inside the primary wall after cell growth; it is thicker and more rigid, and may contain lignin.

items.followUp: What happens to a plant cell when it loses water and its turgor pressure decreases?

rubric.why: Identifies what exerts the pressure and where it acts.
rubric.description: States that pressure is exerted by the cell contents against the cell wall.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the cell contents and cell wall.

rubric.why: Connects turgor pressure with water uptake and a turgid cell.
rubric.description: States that water entering the cell makes it turgid and produces this pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking water uptake with turgidity or pressure.

modelAnswer: Turgor pressure is the pressure exerted by the cell contents against the cell wall when water enters and makes the cell turgid.

items.followUp: During which stage of meiosis does crossing over occur?

rubric.why: Identifies the exchange between homologous chromosomes.
rubric.description: Defines crossing over as the exchange of chromosome segments.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the exchange of segments between homologous chromosomes.

rubric.why: Specifies the chromatids involved and the meiotic context.
rubric.description: States that the exchange occurs between non-sister chromatids during prophase I of meiosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying non-sister chromatids and meiosis (or prophase I).

modelAnswer: Crossing over is the exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis.

rubric.why: Describes the characteristic shape and location of a bleb.
rubric.description: Describes a bleb as a small, bubble-like protrusion of the cell surface or plasma membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the bubble-like protrusion on the cell surface.

rubric.why: Confirms that the structure is a bulge of the membrane.
rubric.description: States that the protrusion is a bulge of the plasma membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as a membrane bulge.

modelAnswer: Blebs are small, bubble-like bulges or protrusions of the plasma membrane on the cell surface.

rubric.why: Identifies the number of chromosome sets in a haploid cell.
rubric.description: States that a haploid cell has one set of chromosomes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one chromosome set or the haploid number n.

rubric.why: Gives a correct example of haploid cells.
rubric.description: Identifies gametes (sex cells) as haploid cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming gametes or sex cells.

modelAnswer: A haploid cell has one set of chromosomes, represented by n.
Gametes are examples of haploid cells.

items.followUp: How does an enzyme affect the activation energy of a reaction?

rubric.why: Names the temporary complex formed during enzyme action.
rubric.description: States that the enzyme binds with its substrate to form an enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming or describing the complex.

rubric.why: States the key benefit of enzyme action.
rubric.description: States that enzyme action lowers activation energy and speeds up the reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the complex helps lower activation energy or increase reaction rate.

modelAnswer: An enzyme binds to its substrate to form an enzyme-substrate complex.
This complex lowers the activation energy, so the reaction proceeds faster.

rubric.why: Explains that activation energy is needed to start a reaction.
rubric.description: States that activation energy is the energy needed to initiate a chemical reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining its role in starting the reaction.

rubric.why: Explains why reactants need an initial energy input.
rubric.description: States that this energy helps weaken or break bonds in the reactants so the reaction can proceed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the energy input with bond weakening or reaction of the reactants.

modelAnswer: Activation energy is necessary to provide the initial energy that starts a chemical reaction.
It helps weaken or break bonds in the reactants so they can undergo the reaction.
